subjects.name: Early years: math and English
subjects.note: Hannah Ward's Little House lessons cover math and English. The Math Ladder's Pre-K course and the pre-reading games are here too, as options.

subjects.name: Math Ladder
subjects.note: Kindergarten to college. Each lesson is a Math Ladder topic: read it, then practice until it passes. Study time is for its quick reviews. Ray's Arithmetic is under More subjects.

courses.name: Today's Math Ladder practice (it picks the next lesson or review)

subjects.name: Writing & Grammar
subjects.note: Age 6 to college: first sentences, grammar and diagramming, usage and punctuation, composition, then rhetoric. Harvey's Grammar and The Mother Tongue are under More subjects.

courses.name: Teach Your Child to Read in 120 Lessons (Hannah Ward)
Phonics Practice (Teddy Rook Book, goes with Hannah Ward's lessons)
Phonics Reading Boot Camp (Hannah Ward), for older learners

subjects.name: Handwriting
subjects.note: Print, then cursive, on the Writing & Grammar Ladder. The Palmer Method is the classic choice in the Book menu.

subjects.name: Biology Ladder
subjects.note: Age 5 to college: seeds, animals and habitats read aloud, then cells, genes, evolution and ecosystems.

subjects.name: Chemistry Ladder
subjects.note: High school to college: atoms, bonds, moles and reactions, with practice that checks every step.

subjects.name: Physics Ladder
subjects.note: Physical Science, then Physics 1 and 2, then college physics. Each lesson is a ladder topic with practice. The Science Lab units are hands-on simulations to add or use on their own.

subjects.name: Earth & Space Ladder
subjects.note: Middle school to college: rocks, plates and volcanoes, oceans, weather and climate, and the planets.

subjects.name: Science
subjects.note: Science Explorers on the Physics Ladder for ages 9 and 10, and the classic science books. The Biology, Physics, Chemistry and Earth & Space Ladders take over where they have a course for the age.

courses.name: The Chemical History of a Candle (chemistry)

subjects.name: Science Lab
subjects.note: Play with the simulations: one idea a session, a different lab each time, with the ladder lesson it goes with. Forty minutes a week is two sessions; raise it for more.

subjects.name: History & Civics
subjects.note: Age 5 to law school: the American story for young learners, U.S. History I and II, civics and government, then law. Stories from History (ages 9 and 10) and Famous Men of Greece and Rome are under History.

subjects.name: History
subjects.note: Stories from History on the History & Civics Ladder for ages 9 and 10, world history told through people and places, and Famous Men of Greece, Rome and the Middle Ages. The History & Civics Ladder takes over for ages 5 to 8 and 13 and up.

courses.name: History & Civics Ladder: Stories from History (ages 9–10)
Famous Men of the Middle Ages

subjects.name: Geography Ladder
subjects.note: Age 5 to AP Human Geography: maps and places, the 50 states, the countries of the world, and how people live on the land.

subjects.name: Art & Drawing Ladder
subjects.note: Age 5 to college: drawing for young artists, drawing basics, color and design, and two art history courses with pictures from the great museums.

subjects.name: Vocabulary Ladder
subjects.note: Grade 6 to adult: the Greek and Latin roots, then 1,000 advanced words with pictures and memory hooks, ten words a topic.

subjects.name: Logic Ladder
subjects.note: Grade 7 to college: informal logic and the fallacies, traditional logic with syllogisms, then symbolic logic with truth tables and proofs.

subjects.name: Economics Ladder
subjects.note: High school to college: microeconomics, macroeconomics and calculus-based micro, then Game Theory and Econometrics.

subjects.name: Debate
subjects.note: Learn to Debate chapter by chapter, then a practice drill each school day. Debate topics, with both sides of each resolution, are in the Book menu. Pairs well with the Logic Ladder.

subjects.name: Test Prep
subjects.note: Practice for the SAT, ACT and CLT: one timed set a school day, math and then reading and grammar.

courses.name: Reading, writing and grammar practice (SAT, ACT and CLT)

subjects.name: Harvard Classics Daily
subjects.note: High school to adult: fifteen minutes a day from Dr. Eliot's Five Foot Shelf, one reading for each school day in the guide's order.

subjects.name: Etiquette Ladder
subjects.note: Age 4 to adult: please and thank you and the family table (read aloud), then conversation, guests and notes, then formal dining, work and life's big occasions.

subjects.name: Egyptology Ladder
subjects.note: Age 8 to college: a first course for young explorers, then the history, religion and art, archaeology, and two courses reading Middle Egyptian hieroglyphs.

subjects.name: Ancient Scripts Ladder
subjects.note: High school to college: Linear A and Linear B, the Bronze Age Aegean, the decipherment and the oldest written Greek.

subjects.name: Memory Ladder
subjects.note: Age 8 to adult: how memory works and the six techniques from "Remember It on Purpose," then the memory systems behind memory challenges. Study time is for its quick spaced reviews.

subjects.name: Great Books Ladder
subjects.note: Age 8 to adult: the Great Books of the Western World, era by era, from Homer to the 20th century. Every rung has a path for young readers, one for teens and adults, and one for going deeper. Study time is for reading.

subjects.name: Robotics Ladder
subjects.note: Age 8 to college: robots for kids with a grown-up, then electronics, programming, mechanics, control and sensing, and college courses in navigation, ROS 2, vision and a capstone. Many lessons have something to build.

subjects.name: Inventors Ladder
subjects.note: Age 9 and up: the inventors in order, from Archimedes to the Wright brothers, with From Scratch builds (a lemon battery, a motor, a telegraph) after the age of electricity, and reading guides to Hawking and Sagan for teens.

subjects.name: Culinary Ladder
subjects.note: Teens and adults: kitchen tools, knife skills and food safety first, then every cooking method, Escoffier's sauces, proteins, pastry, the cold kitchen, flavor, plating and the professional kitchen, with drills to do at home and a capstone tasting menu. Cooking happens with a grown-up for younger teens.

subjects.name: Music
subjects.note: For every age: Piano Basics, then Reading Music, then songs; or choose Guitar, Ukulele or Banjo instead of piano. Study time is practice on the instrument, ten or fifteen minutes most days. The keys on the screen work if you have no piano yet.

courses.name: Play songs (with the rhythm trainer and metronome)

subjects.name: Life skills: Being an Adult 101 and the Trades
subjects.note: Real-world jobs done together: fix a running toilet, check the oil, make a budget. Then how houses and cars work, trade by trade.

subjects.name: Arithmetic
subjects.note: Ray's Arithmetic (1877), an option beside the Math Ladder. Switching the Math Ladder on switches this off; switch it back on to do both.

subjects.name: Algebra and geometry
subjects.note: Ray's Algebra and Wentworth's Geometry, options beside the Math Ladder.

subjects.name: Grammar and composition
subjects.note: Harvey's 1880 grammar, an option beside the Writing & Grammar Ladder. Switching the ladder on switches this off; switch it back on to do both.

subjects.name: Composition
subjects.note: The Mother Tongue (1900), an option beside the Writing & Grammar Ladder.

subjects.name: Bible in a Year
subjects.note: The whole Bible in 365 days, in the order of its story, with a short psalm or proverbs reading each day. Seven readings a school week; on a five-day week, Thursday and Friday have two (tick Saturday and Sunday in step 2 to read one a day). Pick 73 books (Catholic Bibles) or 66 books (most Protestant Bibles) in the Book menu; "From lesson" is the day to start on.

checks.name: Reading
checks.how: Hand your child the screen (or read the lines off it) and ask them to read them aloud to you. Don't help yet; just listen.

checks.name: Spelling
checks.how: Say each word clearly, use it in a short sentence if it helps, and have your child write it down without looking. Then check together.
judge: Spelled them all (or all but one)

checks.name: Arithmetic
checks.how: Let your child work these on paper (or in their head for the first ones). Give no hints; then press “Show answers” and check together.

points.ask: Put out 7 buttons or beans. Ask your child to count them, touching each one, then write the numbers 1 to 10.
lines: Count 7 things, one at a time.
3 boys and 4 girls: how many children?
Sam had 11 marbles and lost 3: how many are left?
One apple costs 6 cents: what do 4 apples cost?
18 pears shared equally by 3 children: how many each?
A pencil costs 6 cents: how much do 9 pencils cost?
